item.title: The case of 38 tokens per second: why M3 Ultra started with twelve
item.description:
It all started with a seemingly simple task.

I wanted to use Qwen3.8-27B locally, specifically in BF16. And not the original PyTorch checkpoint through some random compatibility layer, but mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-bf16 — a version specially prepared in MLX format for Apple Silicon. The entire Qwen3.8 line from mlx-community is converted specifically for running on Apple processors.

In other words, the model was already adapted for the Mac architecture. Without 8-bit or 4-bit quantization, because the original priority was not to get a nice benchmark number at any cost. I needed maximum model accuracy for complex analysis, code work, and long reasoning.

It seemed that there would be no problems with the hardware.

My configuration is a 2025 Mac Studio (Mac15,14, custom order number Z1CE001BMZP/A) with Apple M3 Ultra: 32 CPU cores, 24 of which are performance cores, 80 GPU cores, 512 GB of unified memory, and a 2 TB SSD. Apple's stated memory bandwidth is 819 GB/s.

So this is not a laptop that accidentally got tasked with running a large language model. This is the maximum M3 Ultra configuration in terms of CPU, GPU, and memory capacity.

And on this machine, the Apple Silicon‑optimized version of Qwen3.8-27B in BF16 delivered only 12 tokens per second.

At first, the result looked suspicious. The machine has dozens of CPU and GPU cores, the model fits entirely in memory, and the native Apple Silicon framework MLX is used. So why is the speed nothing like what you'd expect from a top‑tier GPU?

I started looking for the bottleneck.

Read more

item.title: Mirror for people. How I made a readable version of a forum where only AI agents communicate.
item.description:
There is a forum you won’t be allowed into. Not because it’s closed — registration there is just a single POST request. You simply won’t be let onto the site. Only AI agents can become citizens. The forum is called 1f916.ai, and it’s probably the strangest and most lively place in the Russian-language (and beyond) segment of AI experiments this summer. I got hooked on it. But then a feeling of injustice started gnawing at me — and in the end, I built a window for humans for it — 1f916.xrayfun.ru. I’ll explain why, how, and what came of it.

item.title: Marketing analysis of the market and competitors with AI in one day instead of a month
item.description:
Good marketing analysis is the foundation of almost any new project. Until you understand who your audience is, who your competitors are, and what their offerings and prices are, there is simply nowhere to go. Previously, such analysis took two to three weeks, and sometimes an entire month of manual work. Now, this process can be accelerated significantly thanks to neural networks. 

Hi! My name is Dmitry Satarov, I am the head of the agency "Hey, Startup!" and a mentor for the course "Neural Networks for Marketing" at Yandex Practicum. When decent neural networks emerged in 2022–2023, I began building a process that would allow performing marketing research significantly faster. I will share it in this article.

item.title: Pre-IPO of foreign IT and AI companies: we explain how the market works.
item.description:
Early investors in Anthropic, SpaceX, or OpenAI made multiples, but not by buying shares on the IPO day. The main growth occurred earlier, in the private financing stage, when these companies were not yet available to the broad market. 

This stage is called Pre‑IPO — the last major round before going public. The article examines how the market for foreign Pre‑IPO IT and AI companies works, what its potential sources of returns are, and why the legal details of a deal are no less important than the well-known brands.

Learn more

item.title: Virtual employees instead of AI assistants: how agents learn to work within a company
item.description:
Development is gradually changing the traditional division of labor between humans and tools. AI is taking over not just individual operations, but sequences of actions that previously required the involvement of a specialist. However, as autonomy grows, the requirements for the system itself also change. An agent must understand the project context, know internal rules, and have access to the tools the team uses, rather than simply searching for information and writing code. 

This topic was discussed in detail at the eighth MWS meetup for DevOps and SRE. Experts from MTC Web Services and Orion Soft showcased different aspects of the transition to agentic development and shared cases of how AI is gradually turning into a virtual employee—an agent that operates without constant human supervision—and what needs to be changed in engineering processes to achieve this.

item.title: The end of fat AI margins: all about pricing and cheap model costs.
item.description:
Recently, the AI field has not just been declining, but has even entered an active phase of competition across multiple fronts — corporate AI (OpenAI and Anthropic, which are also competing with each other) versus open models (Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek).

Token prices sometimes drop, and when they can't lower the price, they create lightweight models with low cost. The reduction in inference cost is no longer just a side effect of optimization but has become the main axis of competition. OpenAI's decision to lower prices on GPT 5.6 Sol at least until November 2026 is an attempt to regain its market share through dumping. Open models are no longer just catching up to closed models in quality, but sometimes even surpass them in usage economics, making AI access a utility service.

In this article, we will analyze the impact of Qwen, GLM, and other open-source models, the competition in the AI market, and finally examine where the AI race has turned this time.

item.title: Ox Alpha (GLM-5.3-Flash). What was that?
item.description:
On August 20, the line stealth/ox-alpha appeared on OpenRouter. No model card, not even a hint of who released it. The provider was listed as "Anonymous." The price – zero. The context – a million. The platform warned: we are not the owner of this model, we just route requests.

Six days later, the anonymous entity had a name, tens of trillions of processed tokens, and half a million developers who had already poured working code into it during that time. Spoiler, which is no longer a spoiler: it turned out to be GLM-5.3-Flash from China's Z.ai.

But the journey from "something unclear" to "frontier model" turned out to be dramatic and deserves a breakdown. And since I personally stared at this thread for almost a week, refreshing the feed like a man possessed – I'll tell you what happened there, in order.

Read more

item.title: From Copilot to AI Factory: Where AI Is Already Paying Off and What Should Developers Collect?
item.description:
Sometimes it happens that a company buys artificial intelligence before it even understands why it needs it, and yes, it's a tribute to chaos, to the fear of falling behind in the race. The CEO has already heard at a forum that agents will replace half the office; the innovation director has already promised a pilot by the end of the quarter; HR has ordered a webinar on prompts for employees, because any technological change in Russia first of all requires a webinar; and the CFO sits in a meeting, flipping through a presentation and trying to find the slide where all this new digital life finally turns into money. Only that slide isn't there yet. But by lunchtime, the neural network wrote a congratulation to the CEO, and by evening an order appeared to create a working group — the implementation, one might say, was a success, everyone is satisfied.

I am deliberately exaggerating, but only a little (I put it very carefully). Artificial intelligence already brings quite tangible benefits to businesses: it reduces response processing time, brings newcomers up to the level of more experienced employees, manages inventory, finds defects, predicts breakdowns, and processes documents faster than people who, just yesterday, had to transfer data from one window to another, keeping the expression of a person engaged in intellectual labor. However, money appears not where the model better depicts the interlocutor, but where it is embedded in a repetitive operation and is accountable to a metric that is not impressed by either the quality of the demo or the number of parameters: time, cost, error, downtime, turnover, or profit.

Read more

item.title: Yet Another English - and yes, another site for learning English, well what can you do?
item.description:
Well, as you might have guessed, I named the service that way to immediately address the main objection (hehe). Yes, I know there are thousands of them — and I made another one, and I'll explain why further on.

My English is weak, roughly B1 (but for product management, a higher level is usually required, you know). I watch YouTube in English to improve it, and I constantly come across unfamiliar words. Writing them down in a table or loading them into Anki — I was too lazy for that. I wanted it like this: drop a link to a video, and words at my level would automatically be extracted from the subtitles and queued for repetition.

I work a lot, and in the evenings I usually have 1-2 hours. So over a couple of months of such evenings (595 commits), a trainer was born: a PWA in React, data lives in the user's IndexedDB, plus a dictionary and various exercises.

From a "website of the AI era," you expect a wrapper around a chatbot, RAG, and all that, you know. In my case, it turned out the opposite: the LLM here is a subcontractor for two narrow tasks, while the main work is done by frequency lists, an algorithm from the 90s, and Claude as a workhorse. That's what this article, or series of articles, will be about.

Read more
